title: Jeffrey Archer: conviction and public scrutiny
summary: The conviction generated same-day reports, critical profiles and follow-up. The record contradicts a claim of no reporting, while leaving the overall volume and proportionality unmeasured.

anchor.label: A jury at the Central Criminal Court convicted Archer on two counts of perverting the course of public justice and two counts of perjury; he was sentenced to four years' imprisonment. The event followed a seven-week criminal trial.

officialSources.summary: Archer was convicted on 19 July 2001 and sentenced to four years. The House of Lords recorded the court clerk’s notice on 23 July. An obituary is a different editorial event from sentencing.

laterFrame.development: Jeffrey Archer died, aged 86. The official website statement currently available says he died at home the previous day, but does not display a statement publication date in the page text; Associated Press reported on 6 October 2026 that he died on 5 October. Treat this as a separate 2026 obituary/news frame, not as part of the 2001 event-window comparison and not as a proxy for the 2001 coverage volume.
laterFrame.sourceNote: The official site confirms the death and identifies age 86 but does not display a date on the statement text accessed. AP's 6 October 2026 report independently dates his death to 5 October. This fact is explicitly kept outside the 2001 window.

title: Tim Westwood: concerns, institutional response and later reporting
summary: The 2025 review records informal handling of workplace concerns, weak records and missed opportunities. It also found very little evidence that public sexual-misconduct concerns had been reported to the BBC. This supports a specific institutional-response comparison, not a claim that all allegations were known or that no journalism occurred.

title: Cyril Smith: documented non-pickup by major national newspapers
summary: IICSA recorded local articles in May and June 1979, followed by no major-national-newspaper pickup of those allegations. Private Eye and the New Statesman were exceptions. It contacted national papers’ archives without resolving why the story was not taken up. This is documented non-pickup, not an inference from empty searches.

officialSources.locator: Cambridge House, Knowl View and Rochdale report, Part B, paragraphs 62–75; particularly 65–71.

officialSources.title: IICSA report publication record
officialSources.summary: The official report was published 12 April 2018. Its findings about 1979 are retrospective.

limits: The report gives month-level publication dates; no invented daily curve or numerical national-article total is plotted.
The inquiry distinguished documented non-pickup from unresolved explanations. It did not corroborate a D-notice or a supposed legal warning as the cause.
Local publication and two national-magazine exceptions mean this was not complete media silence. This episode is a qualitative comparison, not a matched rate with Jefferies.
Retrospective inquiry findings do not establish exactly what each editor knew in1979, or a general racial/class explanation.
questions: Why did verified local reporting not lead to national scrutiny?
What evidence supports the gap, and what remains unknown about its cause?
When does restraint protect due process, and when can it leave powerful people insufficiently scrutinised?
